text: You tell your AI assistant, “Plan a weekend trip to New York in October.” In seconds, it scans your calendar, finds an open weekend, checks flight options from your preferred airline, books a hotel that matches your taste and loyalty status, and even secures a dinner reservation at a restaurant with both availability and great reviews. It sends the confirmations to your email and syncs everything to your calendar. You gave it a direction—one sentence—and the AI handled the rest. In the workplace, the impact will be even greater. These agents will manage email inboxes, draft replies, summarize meetings, coordinate projects, update CRMs, and even flag conflicting deadlines before you notice them. In law, they’ll prepare the first drafts of contracts. In finance, they’ll generate quarterly reports. In education, they’ll prep lesson plans personalized to each student’s needs. And in customer service, they’ll read every support thread ever written and step in where needed before the customer even knows there’s an issue. These aren’t chatbots. They’re proactive systems with memory, agency, and the ability to learn and adapt. Some will be generalized—like OpenAI’s GPT agents or Google’s Gemini extensions. Others will be specialized, working behind the scenes in logistics, supply chains, and compliance monitoring. They don’t just respond to questions. They anticipate needs. They track your preferences, adapt to your tone, and increasingly coordinate with other agents—your calendar agent, your travel agent, your financial agent—all working in concert like a silent orchestra. This is a very different form of intelligence. Not the kind that speaks to you directly, but the kind that organizes your life, so you have more time to think about and do the things you want to spend your time on. We are entering the age of intelligent delegation. The Interface Mark Zuckerberg and his team at Meta are taking a wearable visual approach: lightweight augmented and virtual reality glasses that could provide persistent, real-time interaction with AI through visual and auditory cues. 87 Meanwhile, as we spoke about earlier, OpenAI made headlines with its partnership with and possible acquisition of Jony Ive’s design firm for a reported $6.4 billion. 88 Under the radar until recently, this stealth collaboration has now been revealed as the foundation for a new kind of device—an AI-native personal companion that Sam Altman has described as “the coolest piece of technology that the world has ever seen.” 89 With this new partnership, OpenAI is signaling that the next paradigm shift may not be software alone, but a rethinking of hardware itself—centered entirely around artificial intelligence, designed not just to be used but to intuitively live alongside us. If the iPhone was the gateway to mobile computing, this may be the gateway to truly ambient AI. Given their collective success, I would keep a very close eye on this model as a next-generation way to plug in with AI, even if, over a longer period of time, something more direct evolves. The Neuralink Interface: From Theory to Reality Elon Musk and others are already successfully developing one potential, yet controversial, answer. Through his company Neuralink, Musk is pioneering the development of brain–computer interfaces (BCIs)—implantable devices designed to create a high-bandwidth, real-time connection between the human brain and digital systems. Why is this so important? If the human brain can compute quickly and efficiently, and AI can compute quickly and at a large scale, then the communication link between the two—which is right now a mouth and a microphone or hands on a keyboard—is the bottleneck. The amount of information per second transmitted through that bottleneck is minuscule. Musk and other BCI champions are trying to broaden the bridge between the two systems so that more traffic can cross per unit of time, allowing them to be more effectively interconnected. 90 The BCI tipping point didn’t happen in a sterile hospital room, but in a lab in the spring of 2021, with Pager, a nine-year-old macaque monkey. 91 Pager was playing a game of Pong, his eyes locked on the screen, his hand manipulating a joystick to chase a dot in exchange for a banana smoothie. Then, the researchers at Neuralink unplugged the joystick. Pager’s hand kept moving, driven by habit, but the physical connection was gone. The paddle on the screen, however, didn’t stop. It continued to glide perfectly to meet the ball, guided no longer by the plastic stick in his hand but by the firing of neurons in his brain. Eventually, the joystick was removed entirely. Pager had been given a Neuralink implant that could read the synaptic signals of his intentions and transmit them to the screen directly—and at the speed of thought. Since that moment with Pager, the program has crossed the threshold from experiment to reality. As of late 2025, a cohort of twelve humans now have the implants and have demonstrated that the barrier between mind and machine is not just thinning; it is dissolving. 92 The progression of this cohort reveals a rapid evolution in how we plug into intelligence. Noland Arbaugh first proved the fundamental thesis: the ability to bypass physical limitations and control a digital cursor with thought alone. 93 He didn’t just move a mouse; he reentered the digital world as an active participant, playing complex strategy games driven purely by neural intent. But the technology quickly moved beyond simple control. Patient Alex pushed the interface from consumption to creation. 94 Where earlier assistive technology was often clumsy or limited to basic inputs, Alex used his implant with the precision required to design 3D objects using professional software. He demonstrated that a brain–computer interface could be a genuine tool for work—removing the friction between the image in his mind and the digital canvas. Perhaps most profoundly, patient Brad demonstrated the restoration of identity. 95 Suffering from ALS and unable to speak, he used the implant to type out text that was instantly vocalized by an AI trained on his original voice.
